messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I encountered a puzzling issue related to the terms for shared partner 
distributions, specifically the directed versions.

I am working with directed networks. Based on the descriptions in the 
reference manual, I thought that Outgoing Two-Paths (OTP) version of 
ddsp (for example) is essentially the same as the original dsp. 
However,  I tend to get different results for the two versions. The same 
goes for the parametric (gw) versions of these terms. I suspect it might 
be a problem with counts in the distribution of shared partners. To 
illustrate what I mean I generated a random directed network (with an 
Erd?s?R?nyi model), and printed summaries using both versions of the dsp 
term. See the result below.

 > summary(net~dsp(0:10))
  dsp0  dsp1  dsp2  dsp3  dsp4  dsp5  dsp6  dsp7  dsp8  dsp9 dsp10
  2420    30     0     0     0     0     0     0     0     0     0

 > summary(net~ddsp(0:10, type = 'OTP'))
  dsp.OTP0  dsp.OTP1  dsp.OTP2  dsp.OTP3  dsp.OTP4  dsp.OTP5 dsp.OTP6  
dsp.OTP7
       -30        30         0         0         0 0         0         0
  dsp.OTP8  dsp.OTP9 dsp.OTP10
         0         0         0

The -30 in the dsp.OTP0 category is wrong, I assume? Is this perhaps a 
problem with the directed versions of the shared partner distributions, 
or is it correct and am I simply overlooking something?

Thank you in advance.

Best,

Wouter Spekkink

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Power analysis for ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael -

Power analysis in the context of dependent data is not trivial, and 
indeed a lot is unknown; ERGMs are no exception.  However, here are some 
practical suggestions:

- In the special case of edgewise independent data, ERGMs reduce to 
logistic network regression, which is nothing more than logistic 
regression where the variables have been expressed as matrices rather 
than vectors.  Standard logistic regression results apply here, and you 
can employ them in the event that you happen to be in this regime.  (In 
particular, note that in this case you have N(N-1)/2 data degrees of 
freedom in the undirected case, and N(N-1) in the directed case, 
assuming no loops.)

- Likewise, dyad (but not edgewise) independent models are akin to 
multinomial logit models on the dyad states, and can be treated accordingly.

- In the more general case, your best bet is probably simulation.  There 
are various ways to proceed, depending on what you want to know - it's 
hard to tell from your description what the specific complaint was, but 
I would look at what, specifically, it is claimed that you would not 
have the power to detect and attempt to assess that by conditional 
simulation.  So, e.g., if you don't find an effect for statistic t, then 
one way to assess how large/small a value t_obs would have been needed 
(holding all else constant) to obtain a significant result at p<k is to 
(1) simulate draws from your model (w/out the t effect), (2) calculate t 
for each draw, and (3) examine the 1-k simulation interval.  (This 
mirrors the type of test for which ERGMs were initially introduced - see 
the later part of Holland and Leinhardt's 1981 JASA paper, on testing 
for triadic effects using p1 as a baseline.)  Other types of questions 
require other procedures, of course.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Devin -

As always, one's first step is to consider what the weights mean (i.e., 
what is being measured?) and make sure that the model one is positing 
makes sense in that light.  There are relatively few relational 
quantities (binding affinities?) I can think of that vary over 4-5 
orders of magnitude, so this is presumably not a typical social system; 
including edge values over such a wide range would seem to imply either 
that they are being normalized by interacting with similarly large 
coefficients as part of some other process (e.g., molar substrate 
quantities in a chemical system, firing events over a long period of 
time in a neural system) or that the response to the edge weight is not 
on the same scale (i.e., a unit increase in edge weight yields much less 
than a unit increase in response at high weight levels).  In the former 
case, one might consider dichotomizing the data (since the low-weight 
edges might as well be zero weight), while in the latter case it might 
be more reasonable to transform the data into a phenomenologically 
reasonable scale.  But it's hard to know how to proceed further without 
knowing more about what the network represents, and what you want the 
model to accomplish.

Hope that helps (by spurring productive questions, at least!),

-Carter

Hi, Mark.  Your question seems to conflate lnam and netlm.  In what 
analysis are you actually interested?  (I would note that neither 
currently has a parallel implementation, but the issues involved in 
parallelizing each are very different.  Also, there are other 
optimizations for large, sparse matrices that can in principle be 
employed for network autocorrelation models that cannot be used for 
netlm, and vice versa.)

As a general matter, just setting aside cores is not going to result in 
performance enhancement for most computation: you have to actually have 
and specifically employ a parallel implementation.  Depending on the 
problem, the difficulty of parallelization can vary from trivial to 
impossible (and it always involves engineering tradeoffs).  But it's 
something that has to be actively designed in.

-Carter

Hello Mateo,

> For the most part, the numbers returned by summary(net ~ term1 + term2 
> +etc.) are straightforwardly interpreted as the count of ties 
> corresponding to that term. Some terms are a bit more obscure.  For 
> example, gwdegree returns a non-whole number. *How is the returned 
> value for gwdegree to be interpreted?*
Indeed, different statistics come in different flavors--some are counts 
of ties, as you mentioned (e.g. edges, nodefactor), others are counts of 
nodes (e.g. degree), or of attribute values (nodecov), of other 
structures (e.g. triangle, cycle).  And then there are the gw* terms.  
They are definitely more complicated than any of the others.  For the 
formal interpretation of any statistic, I'd suggest starting with the 
entry in help("ergm-terms"). In this case, since it's more complicated 
than others, that points you to a few papers: Hunter and Handcock, 2006, 
and Hunter (2007). The definition is in both, but perhaps clearest as 
Equation 14 in Hunter (2007).  Another important paper for understanding 
the theoretical and practical motivations for this and related terms is 
Snijders et al 2006.

Hunter DR, Handcock MS. Inference in Curved Exponential Family Models 
for Networks. Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics. 
2006;15(3):565?583.

Hunter 2007: Hunter DR. Curved Exponential Family Models for Social 
Networks. Social Networks. 2007;29:216?230. 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2031865/

Snijders TAB, Pattison P, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New Specifications for 
Exponential Random Graph Models. Sociological Methodology. 2006;36:99?153.
> A related question: why might there be a discrepancy between the 
> number of edges in the network and the edges value returned by 
> summary()?  I have an undirected network with 2496 edges.  
> Summary(net~edges) returns 1238.  Doubling that to account for 
> non-directedness equals 2476  which is off by 20. All the network 
> default argument values are in place, so there are, for example,  no 
> self-loops that could throw off the count.
I suspect that you've made some mis-steps in the process of converting 
your data from whatever original form you had it in to the network class 
object. As network objects are set up in statnet, you shouldn't have to 
double the number of ties at all - summary should give you 2496, if 
that's how many edges your undirected network is meant to have. The 
easiest way to diagnose this might be if you could explain the original 
form your data came in and all the exact steps (with syntax) that you 
took to convert it to the network object.  Or, even better, if you could 
create a simple example that mimics the process and recreates a version 
of the problem, without having to share your actual data. Of course, if 
you're willing to share your data (with just me, not the whole list), 
then that would make it easiest, but I understand why that's not an 
option for most users.

HTH,
Steve

Hi, Jesse -

Your problem appears to stem from using 
which(expNets[[1]]%e%"effect"==3) to get the edge IDs.  This will only 
work if your edge IDs happen to be exactly the same as their ordering 
(1, 2, 3...).  This is usually the case for newly created network 
objects, but it does not have to be true in general: e.g., your edge IDs 
could be 2, 5, 10, 31, 127, and so forth.  Such "gaps" in edge ID 
sequence usually arise from edges having been deleted from a network 
object at some stage.  As you discovered, the safe way to select edge 
IDs is to use valid.eids() to obtain the ordered list of valid edge IDs, 
and then to subset this list by the output of %e%.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mark -

It sounds like lnam may be what you want (though see below), or an 
equivalent implementation. (There are lots of linear network 
autocorrelation implementations floating around, often under confusingly 
different names.)  I can't speak to how tnam does things (Philip, if you 
are pushing the results to a standard glm function, are you fitting by 
MPLE here?), but indeed the lnam function is hard to parallelize.  It's 
been a while since I looked into this, but IIRC the main bottleneck in 
such algorithms is the determinant calculation (which is needed for the 
normalizing factor in the likelihood function).  If your weight matrix 
is sparse (as is usually the case e.g. for spatial data), there are 
sparse determinant functions that can speed things up; IIRC I have an 
experimental implementation lying around somewhere, but it's not 
thoroughly tested.  However, if you are using geodesics (or functions 
thereof) for your weight matrix, your matrix is probably *not* sparse.  
As I recall, the next trick in line is to use a low-dimensional 
approximation of your matrix to get an (approximate) determinant, which 
will work well when the weights have a sufficiently simple global 
structure.  YMMV.

BTW, as lovely as the network autocorrelation model is from a 
mathematical point of view, it is often a dubious model in practice: it 
is based on pretty strong assumptions about the data generating process 
that may or may not be plausible approximations in any given situation.  
If you have a 6000 node network, do you have reason to think that (1) 
diffusion of your outcome variable actually works the way the model 
assumes, and (2) the system was at least approximately equilibrated when 
measured?  It could well be the best game going for your problem (even 
if imperfect), but you might want to be sure before investing lots of 
time in scaling it.

The other thing that gives me pause is that you say you are looking at 
individual outcomes, while also saying that you are looking at 
"ego/alter association on a trait."  The latter would seem to be a 
relational outcome, not an individual one (and hence my confusion about 
whether you wanted netlm or lnam).  On a fixed network, one could use 
lnams to model edge values (i.e., you are assuming that the network 
topology is fixed on the time scale of the social process, but the 
values of the edges can adjust by interaction with other edges to which 
they are associated in the line graph of the original network), but that 
would be a somewhat unusual application.  For relational outcomes on a 
network that varies on the time scale of the focal process, one would 
usually consider positing a network regression or some other flavor of 
valued ERGM (or, possibly, a latent variable model).  Individual 
outcomes, subject to influence effects, which coevolve on the same time 
scale as the network are very hard, and usually one needs to reach for 
dynamic data to make much headway.  (See, however, Ian Fellows's work 
for some cross-sectional results.)

I think the above counts as more questions than answers, but hopefully 
it is helpful,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Devin.  Pavel provided one useful approach.  Since you are dealing 
with transition matrices, another natural approach would be to 
row-normalize: your i,j cell is then the probability of posting on j 
next, given that one has previously posted on i.  (I would also consider 
using a simple local posterior mean for those probability estimates, 
treating the counts in each row as multinomial and using a minimally 
informative prior - this will give you some shrinkage for extremes in 
the case of small sending groups, and will pull your probability 
estimates away from 0 in the no-observed-transition case.  It's also 
extremely easy to do.)  It would then be natural to work on the logit 
scale, and obvious controls would be column effects (you don't need row 
effects, obviously) and reciprocity.  In principle this can be fit with 
ergm() using the StdNormal reference, although Pavel may want to comment 
on how thoroughly this has been tested to date. Another approach would 
be to fit a latentnet model with receiver effects to control for 
popularity, and then use a permutation test to see if political 
subreddits are closer than would be expected in the residual space.  
(You could put the homophily effect in the model directly, but given the 
issues with accurately estimating the latent versus manifest components 
of latent space models, it's probably just as well to map the subs into 
the latent space and then assess proximity after the fact.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter
